new.definition: A French way with fish: the fillet or whole fish is dusted in flour, cooked in butter, and finished with brown butter, lemon and parsley. The name means in the style of the miller’s wife, and the flour is generally taken to be the point of it. Sole and trout are the classic fish. On the Thanksgiving Day menu it was Redfish Meunière, with brown butter, lemon and capers over a potato and leek écrasé.
new.guest: Meunière, said mun-YAIR, is a classic French way with fish: traditionally dusted in flour, cooked in butter, then finished with brown butter and lemon. The name means in the style of the miller’s wife, for the flour. On Thanksgiving Day ours was redfish, with brown butter, lemon and capers over crushed potatoes and leeks.
new.kitchen: The fish is floured and cooked in hot butter until golden, then the pan butter is taken to a nutty brown and sharpened with lemon at the end. Whether the house floured the redfish, and how the capers went in, was a question for lineup.
new.compare: Amandine is its nearest neighbor: the same floured fish in brown butter, with toasted sliced almonds added. New Orleans menus often join the two as meunière amandine, so the almonds are the tell.

new.background: À la meunière is French for in the style of the miller’s wife, and the usual reading is that the flour on the fish is the miller’s mark, though no record settles where the name began. The style belongs to the French table, with sole and trout its classic fish. Julia Child (1912 to 2004) ate sole meunière at La Couronne in Rouen in November 1948, at her first lunch in France, and later called it the most exciting meal of her life. In New Orleans the style took a Gulf fish. A Tulane University exhibit tells how the founder of Galatoire’s, a cook from near Pau in southwestern France who bought the restaurant in 1905, turned Louisiana speckled trout into trout meunière, and Galatoire’s became known for trout meunière amandine, with toasted almonds in the brown butter.

new.definition: Redfish is the Gulf and Atlantic name for the red drum, Sciaenops ocellatus, a fish of the drum family. Its mark is one large black spot near the base of the tail, sometimes several, which may draw a predator to the tail rather than the head; the Latin ocellatus refers to these eye like spots. It is common from Chesapeake Bay down the Atlantic coast and along the whole American Gulf coast into Mexico. On the Thanksgiving Day menu it was the fish of the Redfish Meunière.
new.guest: Redfish is the red drum, a Gulf Coast fish you know by the black spot near its tail. In New Orleans it is remembered for the blackened redfish craze of the 1980s. On Thanksgiving Day ours was cooked meunière, with brown butter, lemon and capers.
new.kitchen: Louisiana closed its commercial red drum fishery in 1988, and redfish farming, centered in Texas, grew up to supply restaurants. Where the house redfish came from, and how it was cut, was the kitchen’s to say at lineup.
new.compare: Black drum is its nearest neighbor and its cousin in the drum family: a black drum has whisker like barbels under its chin and no tail spot, and a deeper, high backed body, while a redfish is longer, has no barbels and carries the spot at its tail.

new.background: In New Orleans redfish went national through one dish. Paul Prudhomme (1940 to 2015) opened K-Paul’s Louisiana Kitchen on Chartres Street in 1979, and there, in 1980, he began to serve blackened redfish: fillets dipped in butter, coated in a mix of paprika, ground peppers and dried herbs and seared in a very hot iron skillet until a dark crust formed. The dish became a national craze, demand for Gulf redfish soared and the species was badly overfished. Federal regulators closed commercial harvest in the Gulf’s federal waters in 1987, and Louisiana made red drum a recreational fishery only in 1988. Redfish farming, centered in Texas, grew up to supply restaurants.

new.definition: Butter cooked past melting until its water boils away and its milk solids toast to a golden brown, giving a nutty smell and taste. The French call it beurre noisette, hazelnut butter, for its color and aroma. The toasted solids stay in the butter, which is what sets it apart from clarified butter. On the Thanksgiving Day menu it finished the Redfish Meunière and the Sweet Potato Agnolotti, and it went into the spinach of the Turtle Soup.
new.guest: Brown butter is butter cooked gently until it turns golden and smells of toasted hazelnuts; the French call it beurre noisette, hazelnut butter. It gives a warm, nutty richness. On Thanksgiving Day it was on the redfish with lemon and capers, on the sweet potato agnolotti, and in the spinach of our turtle soup.
new.kitchen: The butter melts, foams and sputters while the water cooks off, then goes quiet as the solids start to brown, and from there it darkens fast, so it is watched and taken off the heat the moment it smells nutty. Lemon or other acid goes in at the end for a meunière.
new.compare: Beurre noir is its nearest neighbor: black butter, cooked further until the solids are very dark, then sharpened with lemon or vinegar. Clarified butter goes the other way, with the milk solids taken out so nothing browns. Golden solids and a hazelnut smell are the tell of brown butter.

new.background: Brown butter asks only butter and heat. The French name, beurre noisette, means hazelnut butter, for the color of the browned solids and the nutty smell. Taken further it becomes beurre noir, black butter, sharpened with lemon or vinegar and served with eggs, fish and vegetables. With lemon and parsley, brown butter is the meunière sauce of the classic sole and trout. The science came later. The flavor comes from the milk solids, whose sugars and amino acids react as they toast. That browning bears the name of the French physician and chemist Louis Camille Maillard (1878 to 1936), who described the reaction of amino acids with sugars in 1912.

new.definition: French for crushed: on a menu, a dish of cooked vegetables crushed with a fork or masher rather than puréed smooth, most often potatoes. It is a rustic, chunkier cousin of mashed potatoes, keeping some texture and often enriched with butter or olive oil. French cooks also call it pommes de terre à la fourchette, potatoes done with the fork. On the Thanksgiving Day menu a potato and leek écrasé sat under the Redfish Meunière.
new.guest: Écrasé, said ay-krah-ZAY, is French for crushed: potatoes crushed with a fork rather than whipped smooth, so they keep a little texture. On Thanksgiving Day ours was potato and leek, under the redfish meunière, and it soaked up the brown butter.
new.kitchen: The potatoes are cooked until tender and crushed while hot, by fork or masher, with the fat worked in lightly so they stay coarse rather than gluey. What went into the house écrasé besides potato and leek, and how the leeks were cooked, was the kitchen’s to say.
new.compare: Pommes purée is its nearest neighbor: a purée is pressed through a ricer or sieve and worked with butter until silky and smooth, while an écrasé is only crushed and keeps its lumps. Texture is the tell.

new.background: Écrasé is the past participle of the French verb écraser, to crush, which Merriam-Webster traces to Middle French ecraser. The Académie française gives, among the verb’s first senses, crushing potatoes to make a purée, and Le Robert records écrasé as a noun of the kitchen, a dish of a crushed food, as in un écrasé de pommes de terre. French cooks also speak of pommes de terre à la fourchette, potatoes crushed with a fork and often dressed with olive oil, and on a French menu an écrasé de pommes de terre names a coarser, rustic style than the smooth purée. The potato itself came late to French tables: the Paris Faculty of Medicine declared it fit to eat in 1772, helped by the campaign of Antoine Augustin Parmentier (1737 to 1813).

new.definition: A member of the onion family, Allium ampeloprasum, grown for its long white shank rather than a bulb. Growers hill soil around the stalk as it grows to keep it pale, and since leeks grow in sandy soil, grit tends to hide between the layers. The white and light green parts are the tender ones, with a taste like a mild, sweet onion that cooking softens further. On the Thanksgiving Day menu leeks were crushed with potato in the écrasé under the Redfish Meunière.
new.guest: A leek is a gentle cousin of the onion, long and white with a mild, sweet flavor that turns soft and silky when cooked. Potato and leek are an old French pairing, the pair behind leek and potato soup. On Thanksgiving Day they were crushed together under the redfish meunière.
new.kitchen: Leeks are trimmed of roots and coarse dark tops, which can go to stock, then split lengthwise and rinsed with the layers fanned, or sliced and soaked so the grit sinks. How the house cooked the leeks for the écrasé was a question for lineup.
new.compare: The onion is its nearest neighbor: an onion swells into a bulb with a sharper bite, while a leek grows a long blanched shank and tastes milder and sweeter. The long white stalk is the tell.

new.background: Leeks are an old food. Dried remains, carvings and wall drawings show them in the Egyptian diet from at least the second millennium BC. Rome prized them: Pliny the Elder, who died in 79, wrote that the emperor Nero (37 to 68) ate leeks with oil on set days each month for the sake of his voice. The leek is a national emblem of Wales, beside the daffodil, and was traditionally worn on Saint David’s Day; the story of Welsh soldiers wearing leeks into battle is told in several versions, none of them settled. In France leek and potato soup, potage Parmentier, is a staple of the home kitchen, and Louis Diat (1885 to 1957), the French born head chef of the Ritz Carlton in New York, is credited with serving it chilled with cream as vichyssoise, usually dated to 1917.

deepen.background: Green beans are the young pods of the common bean, Phaseolus vulgaris, which was domesticated in the Americas at least twice, in Mesoamerica and in the Andes, from about 8,000 years ago. The bean crossed to Europe after Columbus; the first sure evidence there dates to the middle of the 1500s, and the first European picture of it appeared in the herbal of Leonhart Fuchs (1501 to 1566) in 1542. Where the French word haricot comes from is still argued: English dictionaries lean to the Nahuatl ayacotli, with the spelling shaped by an older French haricot, a stew of cut up meat, while French dictionaries derive the bean’s name from that stew itself. On a menu the name now means the slender filet type, and French sources list among the filet beans the fin de Bagnols and the triomphe de Farcy.
deepen.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: the Haricots Verts side
deepen.guest: Haricots verts, said ah-ree-koh VAIR, are French green beans: thinner and more tender than the everyday kind, picked young while the pod is slender. Cooked briefly, they stay bright green with a little snap. On Thanksgiving Day they were the green side for the table, a fresh contrast to the turkey and the stuffing.
